blocks.text: This book is a novel. Aya, Andrés, Lía, Nexum Biogenetics and the Cartagena of 2060 are fiction. What follows is not. Here we separate, as carefully as we can, what already existed in 2026 (with dates and sources) from what still belongs to the realm of speculation or dreams. Nothing written in these pages is a substitute for the judgement of a healthcare professional.

blocks.text: **Artificial intelligence already helps us understand proteins.** In 2021, the AlphaFold system, developed by researchers at DeepMind, showed that a neural network can predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein from its amino-acid sequence with an accuracy that, in many cases, approaches that of experimental methods. The work of John Jumper, Demis Hassabis and the rest of the team was published in *Nature* on 15 July 2021, under the title “Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold” (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03819-2). This does not mean that an artificial intelligence “designs life” on its own, or cures diseases simply by naming them. It means that part of the problem biologists call “protein folding” has, for the first time, a computational tool of extraordinary power, and that this tool is already used in laboratories all over the world to research drugs and disease mechanisms.

blocks.text: **Medicine is beginning to adjust to each person's DNA.** So-called precision medicine (or personalised medicine) is not a slogan from 2060: it is an approach that regulatory agencies themselves describe today. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) defines it as a way of tailoring prevention and treatment to the differences in each person's genes, environment and lifestyle, with the aim of giving “the right treatment to the right patient at the right time” (https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/in-vitro-diagnostics/precision-medicine). A concrete example is pharmacogenomics, which studies how DNA influences the response to a medicine: whether a drug will suit someone, whether a different dose will be needed, or whether another therapy should be chosen. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) explain this on their official page on pharmacogenomics (https://www.cdc.gov/genomics-and-health/pharmacogenomics/index.html). In 2026, this approach is already used for some medicines, not all, and it is nothing like a “tomato” that makes a made-to-measure cure at home.

blocks.text: **Gene editing already has approved therapies, not just experiments.** On 8 December 2023, the FDA approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first therapy authorised in the United States that uses the CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technique, to treat sickle cell disease in patients aged 12 and over with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapies-treat-patients-sickle-cell-disease). In the European Union, Casgevy received a conditional marketing authorisation on 9 February 2024, for transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia and for severe sickle cell disease in certain patients from that same age, according to the official page of the European Medicines Agency (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/casgevy). It is a real milestone. It is also a complex, hospital-based therapy, subject to additional monitoring, not a magical correction at the touch of a hand.

blocks.text: **Some medicines can already be produced in plants, but not the “tomato of life” in this book.** On 1 May 2012, the FDA approved Elelyso (taliglucerase alfa), an enzyme replacement therapy for type 1 Gaucher disease, manufactured in genetically modified carrot cells, according to the approval file (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2012/022458Orig1s000Approv.pdf). This shows that “molecular farming” in plant cells exists and has reached an authorised drug. It does not show that there are personalised tomatoes, grown for the DNA of a single person, capable of healing with no owner and no price. In the novel, that is Lía's dream. In 2026, it is still a dream.

blocks.text: What Is Not Yet Possible in Humans
blocks.html: What Is Not Yet Possible in Humans

blocks.text: **A mammal can be born, in the laboratory and in mice, with genetic material from two mothers or, with far greater difficulty, from two fathers. In humans, no.** On 22 April 2004, *Nature* published the work of Tomohiro Kono and his colleagues, “Birth of parthenogenetic mice that can develop to adulthood” (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature02402). The team obtained a viable mouse, known as Kaguya, from two maternal genomes, by combining a modified immature oocyte with a mature oocyte. Kaguya reached adulthood and was able to reproduce in the conventional way. The study itself shows that the usual barrier is genomic imprinting: in mammals, some genes are expressed differently depending on whether they come from the father or the mother, which is why single-sex reproduction does not occur naturally.

blocks.text: On 11 October 2018 (in the 1 November 2018 issue of *Cell Stem Cell*), Zhi-Kun Li, Wei Li, Qi Zhou and their team published “Generation of Bimaternal and Bipaternal Mice from Hypomethylated Haploid ESCs with Imprinting Region Deletions” (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stem.2018.09.004). Using haploid embryonic stem cells and the deletion of imprinting regions, they produced mice with two mothers that reached adulthood and were able to reproduce, and also mice with two fathers; the latter were born with serious abnormalities and died shortly after birth. The contrast matters: a headline is not the same as an animal that lives.

blocks.text: On 15 March 2023, *Nature* published “Generation of functional oocytes from male mice in vitro”, by Kenta Murakami, Katsuhiko Hayashi and the rest of the group (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05834-x). The team managed to convert pluripotent cells from male (XY) mice into XX cells, differentiate them into functional oocytes and, after fertilisation, obtain offspring. It is a notable advance in in vitro gametogenesis in mice. It is not yet a method that can be applied to people.

blocks.text: **In humans, today, these routes are neither possible nor authorised.** Human genomic imprinting is more complex than that of the mouse, and there is no clinical, safe and accredited technique for conceiving a child from a single parent, or from two parents of the same sex without gametes of the other sex. In Spain, moreover, the legal framework in force in 2026 does not authorise such practices. Law 14/2006 of 26 May on assisted human reproduction techniques permits only scientifically accredited and clinically indicated techniques, and expressly prohibits “the cloning of human beings for reproductive purposes” (Article 1.3) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-9292). Law 14/2007 of 3 July on Biomedical Research prohibits “the creation of human pre-embryos and embryos exclusively for experimental purposes” (Article 33.1) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2007-12945). The Oviedo Convention, done on 4 April 1997 and ratified by Spain (instrument published in the BOE on 20 October 1999; in force since 1 January 2000), states in Article 13 that an intervention seeking to modify the human genome may only be undertaken for preventive, diagnostic or therapeutic purposes, “and only if its aim is not to introduce any modification in the genome of any descendants” (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1999-20638). (The quotations from the two Spanish laws are our own translation; the Oviedo Convention is quoted from its official English text.)

blocks.text: This novel imagines that, by 2060, some of those prohibitions are being debated or have changed, because the laws and ideas of one era do not always coincide with those of the next. That is a premise of fiction, not a prophecy. We do not know what a fair law of 2026 will be in 2060. What we do know is what is permitted today, what is not, and what science still cannot do.

blocks.text: **Nor do cultivated human wombs or a complete artificial gestation exist in 2026.** The closest thing, and even then in animals and for a different purpose, is research into extra-uterine environments for extremely premature lambs. On 25 April 2017, Emily A. Partridge, Alan W. Flake and their colleagues published the article “An extra-uterine system to physiologically support the extreme premature lamb” in *Nature Communications* (https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15112), describing a closed system, the so-called “biobag”, able to support for up to four weeks lamb foetuses equivalent in development to an extremely premature human baby. The declared aim is to help babies who are born too early, not to manufacture a body from scratch or replace an entire pregnancy. In 2026, this is not routine clinical practice in people, much less a “laboratory womb” like Aya's.

blocks.text: **Eternal life is not an approved therapy.** There is serious research on ageing, but there is no authorised medicine or procedure that halts death or grants a life without end. In Chapter 9, that promise appears as a temptation, not as a fact. It is worth saying clearly, so that a character's desire is not mistaken for a fact.

blocks.text: In the novel, Lía doesn't only heal: she asks who decides what counts as a flaw. That question is ethical, not technical, and it cannot be settled by a scientific paper. The science of 2026 can already predict proteins, adjust some drugs to DNA and, in very specific cases, edit the genome of a patient's cells to treat a serious disease. Everything else (the daughter of a human and a chip-mind, the personal tomato, the correction of an entire life, eternity) belongs to the imagination. Imagination is good for thinking. It is not, on its own, good for prescribing.
